name: Chlorine dioxide rinse

lead: A chlorine dioxide rinse is a mouthwash with stabilized chlorine dioxide as the active ingredient, sold to reduce bad breath. Users in breath-focused circles favor it because it is alcohol-free and acts chemically on odor compounds.
An 8-week randomized trial tested it against a placebo rinse in people with intrinsic oral malodor, and Wikipedia cites a meta-analysis reporting benefit for halitosis.

paras: Chlorine dioxide is an oxidizer. The proposed mechanism is oxidation of volatile sulfur compounds, the odorous molecules produced by oral bacteria.

Dilute oral rinsing is accepted in mouthwash use, but concentrated chlorine dioxide is toxic. The FDA warns against ingesting chlorine-dioxide products marketed as cures, which have caused serious injury.

lead: A chlorine dioxide rinse is an alcohol-free mouthwash that contains stabilized chlorine dioxide, an oxidizing agent, as its active ingredient. It is marketed mainly for oral malodor (bad breath), and its proponents say it works by chemically neutralizing the volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs) responsible for much of the odor.[1][2]

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial published in 2018 tested an unflavored, non-fluoridated, alcohol-free stabilized chlorine dioxide mouthwash over eight weeks in healthy people with clinically diagnosed intrinsic oral malodor, using it as an adjunct to tooth brushing.[1] Wikipedia notes that dilute chlorine dioxide is an antiseptic ingredient in some mouthwashes and cites a meta-analysis reporting that daily use is effective for halitosis.[2]

Chlorine dioxide is also a toxic industrial chemical, and the US Food and Drug Administration has warned against ingesting chlorine-dioxide products marketed as cures, a different use from supervised dilute oral rinsing.[2]
infobox: Limited: small number of randomized trials

paras: Chlorine dioxide is a strong oxidizer. Manufacturers and proponents describe the rinse as oxidizing odor-causing volatile sulfur compounds, rather than simply masking them with flavoring.[1] The 2018 trial deliberately used an unflavored formulation versus a placebo rinse, consistent with testing the active ingredient itself rather than flavor effects.[1]

At the dilute concentrations used in mouthwash, chlorine dioxide is considered an acceptable antiseptic ingredient, according to Wikipedia's summary.[2] The compound in concentrated or gaseous form is toxic and can decompose explosively, so it is normally handled as a dilute aqueous solution.[2]

The FDA has stated that internal use of chlorine dioxide products has no health benefits, with dilute supervised oral rinsing as the exception, and has issued warnings about products such as Miracle Mineral Solution. Fraudulent marketing of chlorine dioxide as a cure for conditions including autism and COVID-19 has led to documented serious harm.[2] These products are distinct from commercial mouthwashes.

An 8-week, single-site, two-way crossover randomized controlled trial compared a stabilized chlorine dioxide mouthwash with a placebo mouthwash as an adjunct to brushing in healthy subjects with clinically diagnosed intrinsic oral malodor.[1] Wikipedia additionally cites a meta-analysis concluding that daily use of chlorine dioxide rinse is effective for treating halitosis.[2] The body of published trials is small, and results are specific to the products tested.
